conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. I see you came in because your GJ tube was pulled out this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I didn’t mean to. I was moving and it came out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve placed a temporary tube to keep the opening safe. It’s called a Foley catheter, and it’s in your stomach right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get my regular tube back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Interventional Radiology will replace your GJ tube tomorrow. It’s a quick procedure under imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just want to get back to my meds and feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you don’t miss anything. For now, you’re getting fluids through an IV, and we gave you a dose of metoprolol because your heart rate was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart? It’s been fast before…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. It’s likely from missing your morning dose and being a bit dehydrated. The IV fluids should help, and we’ll keep you on your usual metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I take a lot of meds… for HIV, seizures, breathing…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed all your medications. You’re on Truvada, darunavir, and ritonavir for HIV, Keppra for seizures, and your breathing meds like albuterol. We’ll continue all of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach pain? It’s been off and on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your abdomen. It’s soft, no tenderness. We’ll keep you on hyoscyamine and cholestyramine for your chronic diarrhea and discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had loose stools again today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We won’t give extra constipation meds unless needed. Your body is adjusting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your lab results. Your white blood cell count was high when you arrived—17,000—but it’s already coming down to 13,000.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but you’re not running a fever or showing other signs. You have a long-term Foley catheter, which often causes bacteria in the urine without being a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. Your urine culture showed mixed bacteria, which means it’s likely contamination. We won’t treat it since you’re not symptomatic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows mild fluid in the lungs, but no pneumonia. It’s likely related to your chronic lung disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had COPD for years… and the trach helps, but I need suctioning a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re suctioning as needed and giving albuterol if you’re short of breath. Keep using the voice box when you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling? Any pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stomach feels okay. Still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. You’ll rest tonight, and tomorrow morning the GJ tube will be replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well last night. Your heart rate is down to 69, and your breathing is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Is it time for the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The radiology team replaced your GJ tube this morning under X-ray guidance. It’s in the right place and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No incision. They used a wire and a new tube over it. You were given light sedation and tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start my feeds and meds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start slow. The nurse will begin your medications through the tube, then your feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with your sister and the nursing home. They said your Foley catheter was kept in place until you finished treatment for a past infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had it for over a year…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend removing it soon. It increases infection risk. You could use a condom catheter or urinal instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll talk to the nurse at the home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go back to the extended care facility today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back so soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your tube is fixed, your labs are improving, and you’re stable. Just keep up with your HIV meds, breathing treatments, and follow up with cardiology about your heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking it twice a day. But talk to electrophysiology—they can decide if you need it long-term or an ablation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we reviewed your code status with your sister. She said you want full treatment if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I want everything done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. Your care team will respect that. You’ll be discharged in the next few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is ready. Remember to keep your GJ site clean, take all your meds, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All right. Stay well, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Have a safe trip back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—discharge orders are complete. You’re officially discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. See you later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you made it to transport safely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Rest well.
